# 25-26 DC Report

# VAWT basics 

## **VAWTs vs HAWTs**

- HAWTs require consistent wind parallel to the axis of rotation  
  - Usually in remote or offshore locations  
  - Have self-starter and a yaw system to align with wind direction  
  - Efficiencies around 40-55%  
- VAWTs are omnidirectional, lower cut-in speed, but less efficient, not widely used  
  - Efficiencies around 20-40% depending on type


![][image1]

- ## **Urban environments disrupt airflow** due to their increased surface roughness

  - Lower wind speed  
  - Regions w high local velocity and high density  
  - Rapid changes in flow direction \-\> increased turbulence \-\> high load on WTs  
- Putting a bunch together can increase their power output bc of how the air vortices created by the blades interact

## **Power and parameters**

- Pwind \= 0.5⍴SU3 (⍴ \- density of air, S \- swept area (H\*D), U \- air velocity)

![][image2]

- Cut in speed: wind speed at which the turbine starts rotating  
- Rated speed: wind speed at which turbine generates max possible power  
- Cut out speed: speed at which the turbine is stopped to prevent damage  
- Starting torque: torque generated before turbine begins rotating  
  - Turbine can self start if the starting torque \> static friction in bearings

![][image3]

# CFD

- Divides continuous fluid domain into small discrete cells (meshing) where governing equations are solved at specific locations  
- Requires very careful set up and calibration to ensure accurate results  
- Set up / process  
  - Import turbine geometry from CAD software  
  - Define computational domain – large enough to reduce impact of artificial boundaries  
  - Divide into inner rotating domain including turbine, and outer stationary domain  
  - Turbine rotation will be constant at a set angular velocity (regardless of air forces)  
    - can be set up w/ AMI or MRF  
  - Select turbulence model  
  - Specify boundary conditions and initial conditions  
  - MUST HAVE A HIGH QUALITY MESH FOR GOOD RESULTS  
  - They did a mesh sensitivity analysis with a steady state model and increasing mesh fineness to determine when the moment coefficient converged to a single value

# Darrieus VAWTs

- Lift-based: generate electricity using lift to turn the rotor  
  - Airfoil shaped blades  
  - Wind flow creates high pressure zone on one side of the blade, low pressure on the other → lift perpendicular to the wind direction

  ![][image4]

- Can rotate much faster than free stream wind velocity —\> TSR \> 1  
- More efficient than drag-based Savonius turbines  
  - Efficiencies \~30-40%  
- **Usually can’t self start which is their biggest issue**  
    
- Different types have different self-starting abilities, torque consistency, and manufacturability  
  - D type (eggbeater)  
  - H type: uniform angle of attack  
  - Helical type

- ## **Blade pitch and angle of attack**

  - If you change the blade’s pitch angle the angle of attack changes and torque can be increased  
  - Attack angle must remain less than the stalling angle  
    - Stall angle (aka critical angle of attack) determined by lift coefficient curve of the airfoil  
    - Optimal between 4-10 deg

- ## **Airfoil type**

  - Symmetrical NACA airfoil profiles are most common  
    - Thickness ratios (max thickness:chord length) between 12-21%  
      - Can be used to optimize stable performance and reduced drag  
    - well documented aerodynamic characteristics and predictable behavior

# Savonius VAWTs

- Drag based  
  - Cannot rotate faster than wind speed → 0 \<= TSR \<= 1

  ![][image5]

  - Simple construction and installation  
  - Inexpensive  
  - Work at low wind speeds   
  - Can self start  
  - Low operating speed \= quiet  
  - Lots of negative torque though so very inefficient


- ## **Hybrid turbines**

  - Combo to combat the weaknesses of sav and dar turbines  
  - Often w/ outer darrieus and inner savonius but there are different configurations  
  


  


  


  


  


  


  


- **Num stages**  
  - Num of individual rotors are stacked (usually not more than 3\)  
  - 3 stage rotors improve self starting but decrease coefficient of power (vs 1 stage)  
- **Num blades (n)**  
  - Optimal num blades is indep of num stages  
  - Two blades produces more power than three blades  
- **Overlap ratio (OR)**  
  - Distance of overlap between the two blades / chord length  
  - Wind passing through the gap increases with more blade overlap  
    - Wind passing through flows through the concave side of the returning blade and produces more thrust  
  - No agreed upon optimal OR but most studies say OR between 0.1 and 0.3 are ideal, and 0.15 is a frequently cited number.   
- **Aspect ratio (AR)**  
  - AR \= H / D  
  - Larger aspect ratio increases power coefficient  
  - Other studies showed best results at 0.7 or between 1.5-2  
  - Most existing rotors have ARs near 1.0 for structural reasons  
- **Blade shape**

- A study analyzing helical-shaped savonius turbines found a blade twist angle of 45 deg to be best and 90 to be worse than 0  
- Tapered blade tips have also been shown to improve power output

  ![][image6]


- Augmentation devices  
  - Direct or block wind to/from different parts of turbine blades  
  - Endplates  
    - Prevents air from escaping the tips of the concave side of both blades  
    - Can vary the ratio of endplate diameter to blade diameter to max power  
  - shielding obstacles  
    - Deflect wind from returning blades to decrease negative torque   
  - Guiding vanes  
    - Direct incoming wind towards advancing blade  
    - Provide a funneling effect to accelerate wind upstream of rotor  
    


- Mini / quarter blades  
  - Placed concentrically within rotor blades to increase efficiency

# Areas to Improve

## **Optimization opportunities for VAWTs:**

- **Reduce cut in speed** to increase starting torque and self-starting ability, and general application in low wind speed environments  
- **Increase efficiency** esp in turbulent conditions to increase functionality in urban environments  
- **Reduce noise and vibration** to minimize impact on people living/working nearby  
- **Reduce initial cost** to increase market, and **improve overall quality** to reduce maintenance costs/improve lifetime  
- **Reduce stalling** in high wind speeds

## **Considerations for future work:**

- Continue w/ low wind speed application (like Smith) and improve design efficiency  
- Shift to higher wind speed applications like top of skyscrapers  
- Focus on CFD and digital twin

# Fluids concepts

**Venturi effect \+ aerodynamic drag \-**   
[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GMmNKUlXXDs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GMmNKUlXXDs) 

CoM and CoE explain a venturi \- in order to conserve mass, when the pipe narrows the flow must speed up. Then, to conserve energy, in the faster flowing region, the pressure must drop (Bernoulli’s). This explains boundary layers around objects in flowing fluid. With a fairly blunt object like a sphere, the fluid flowing past it speeds up as it approaches the top/bottom of the sphere since it is being squeezed past the free stream fluid and the sphere’s surface. The pressure gradient here is favorable (decreasing). Then, as the fluid passes towards the back of the sphere, it slows down and the pressure increases. At some point the increasing pressure will force some of the slow moving fluid next to the surface to reverse direction and separate from the sphere’s surface. This creates a wake and a low pressure area behind the sphere. When the separation occurs depends on if the boundary layer was laminar or turbulent. See below.

### **Laminar vs turbulent boundary layers \-** 

[https://www-mdp.eng.cam.ac.uk/web/library/enginfo/aerothermal\_dvd\_only/aero/fprops/introvisc/node8.html](https://www-mdp.eng.cam.ac.uk/web/library/enginfo/aerothermal_dvd_only/aero/fprops/introvisc/node8.html)   
Turbulent flow mixes more efficiently than laminar which results in the exchange of mass, momentum, etc. This is why a turbulent boundary layer can resist separating more than a laminar boundary layer, since momentum will be mixed which lets the air closest to the surface resist the adverse pressure gradient longer. See golf balls and dimples.

### **Skin (viscous) drag vs form (pressure) drag \- [https://www.comsol.com/blogs/why-do-golf-balls-have-dimples](https://www.comsol.com/blogs/why-do-golf-balls-have-dimples)** 

Dimples on a golf ball are helpful because the form drag \>\>\>\> skin drag, dimples disrupt the boundary layer and make it turbulent which reduces form drag and therefore overall drag

For application to VAWT blades, this would only be helpful if the form drag is more of a problem than skin drag. But the blades are usually tapered so they’re more aerodynamic which reduces the form drag so dimples/texture might not be useful.

### **Static and dynamic stall \-** 

[https://www.flyaeroguard.com/learning-center/airfoil-stalls/](https://www.flyaeroguard.com/learning-center/airfoil-stalls/) 

If the angle of attack is too large the boundary layer separates much closer to the leading edge of the airfoil which dramatically reduces lift and increases drag. As the blades of an H type darrieus VAWT rotate, the AOA changes, so with fixed blades there is only one point of their path with an ideal AOA and depending on the TSR there may or may not be a point where dynamic stall occurs. This causes a lot of mechanical stress in addition to the loss of lift.
